title: Don't become the judge
hook: The more you learn, the easier it is to notice what everyone else is doing wrong. Let's talk about that.

screens.text: Ten weeks ago you didn't know how to pray. Now you know a lot. And you might catch yourself thinking: "Her hijab isn't right." "He never comes to the masjid." "My cousin's going to regret that." Today is about that voice.

**A trap that catches eager Muslims.** New knowledge can quietly turn into a ruler for measuring everyone else. Many converts say harsh judging pushed them away from the masjid. Many also admit they became the judge for a while [Field Guide ch. 17].
bubbles: The Prophet ﷺ described arrogance as rejecting the truth and looking down on people. Even a mustard seed of it is serious [Muslim 91].

screens.prompt: How did the Prophet ﷺ describe arrogance?
screens.answer: Rejecting the truth and looking down on people
screens.feedback: That's it [Muslim 91]. Judging others from above is one of its signs.

screens.text: **Only Allah sees the heart.** The Prophet ﷺ said Allah doesn't look at our looks or our wealth, but at our hearts and our deeds [Muslim 2564].
bubbles: The Qur'an says: *"do not claim yourselves to be pure; He is most knowing of who fears Him"* [Q 53:32, Saheeh Intl.].
He also told of a woman with a sinful past who was forgiven for giving water to a dog dying of thirst [Bukhari 3321].

cards.back: "I don't know her journey. Mine isn't finished either." Hijab can be a long road, and nobody's faith is measured by one thing you can see.
"He came. That's a door open." A warm salam may be why he comes back next week.
"I didn't know any of this a year ago either." Be kind, make du'a for them, and let your character speak.

cards.front: "I'm doing better than most people here."
cards.back: That one's the ego talking. Nobody knows where they stand with Allah. Hope and humility, for yourself and everyone.

screens.situation: At a work party, Luis notices Aaliyah, another Muslim, has a glass of wine. Nobody else knows she's Muslim. He feels his face get hot.

options.text: Say nothing in front of others. Later, if they're close enough, a short private and kind word, said once. Then make du'a for her.
options.feedback: Yes. Private, gentle, one time, with real care. And he keeps her secret, as he'd want his kept.
Not quite. Exposing someone in public humiliates her and helps no one. Allah covers the one who covers others [Bukhari 2442].

options.text: Tell the other Muslims at work so they know
options.feedback: Not quite. That's spreading her private struggle. Mocking or exposing others is something the Qur'an warns against [Q 49:11].

options.text: Decide she's not a real Muslim and stop talking to her
options.feedback: Not quite. Struggling isn't leaving Islam. She may need a kind friend more than anything.

screens.title: When advice is really needed
screens.intro: Caring is different from judging. Sometimes a word of advice is right. When it is:

steps.text: **Gentle**, the way you'd want to hear it

screens.text: **Keep people's faults covered.** The Prophet ﷺ said whoever covers a fellow Muslim, Allah will cover him on the Day of Judgment [Bukhari 2442].
bubbles: Everyone, you included, is walking around covered by Allah.

items.text: A short, kind word to a friend, in private, said once
items.why: Private, gentle, once. Then leave it with Allah.

items.text: Correcting someone loudly in front of everyone
items.why: Public correction humiliates. Advice is private and gentle.

items.text: Telling your friends about a Muslim's slip
items.why: That uncovers a fault. Whoever covers a Muslim, Allah covers him [Bukhari 2442].

items.text: Making a quiet du'a for someone instead of grumbling about them
items.why: That's care. You want good for them, not to be right.

screens.prompt: Think of a moment you judged someone, Muslim or not, in the last few weeks. What was going on for you? What might have been going on for them?

chips: When should I actually say something to someone?
Someone at the masjid keeps judging me. What do I do?
How do I stop feeling better than my family?
Isn't it my duty to correct wrong things?

screens.text: Swap one judging thought for a du'a.
steps: Next time a judging thought comes, make a short du'a for that person instead, in your heart
Try it at least once today
screens.optional_extra: Make a du'a for yourself too: that Allah keeps your heart humble and covers your faults.

screens.text: Only Allah sees hearts. Work on yourself, be gentle with others, and keep their faults covered.
Your job isn't to grade anyone. It's to be kind and keep growing.

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- Arrogance is rejecting the truth and looking down on people; even a mustard seed of it is grave [Muslim 91]. The same hadith says Allah is beautiful and loves beauty, so caring about appearance isn't arrogance.
- Allah looks at hearts and deeds, not looks or wealth; a Muslim doesn't look down on his brother [Muslim 2564].
- Don't claim purity for yourselves; Allah knows best who is mindful of Him [Q 53:32].
- A woman with a sinful past was forgiven for watering a thirsty dog [Bukhari 3321].
- Don't ridicule others; they may be better than you [Q 49:11]. Whoever covers a Muslim, Allah covers him on the Day of Judgment [Bukhari 2442].
- Field Guide ch. 17: converts who learn quickly can slide into harshness; good advice is private and kind, and the five-step reset (stop, repent, ask Allah's help, thank Him for covering your faults, extend mercy) [Field Guide ch. 17].
- Harsh correction is one of the main reasons converts feel pushed away [Research Notes - Retention and Convert Voices, theme 3].

**Likely questions**
- *"Isn't it my duty to correct wrong things?"* Yes, enjoining good is part of Islam, but with knowledge, wisdom and gentleness, in private, and only where you're sure it's actually wrong (not a difference between schools). A few months in, the best tools are your example and du'a. Big situations: ask the imam.
- *"Someone keeps judging me."* Validate the hurt. Their harshness isn't Islam. Options: a calm "Thanks, I'm learning at my own pace," talk to the mentor or imam, sit with kinder people. They don't have to accept being humiliated.
- *"I feel superior to my non-Muslim family now."* Gently: a year ago they were where you were. Being chosen for guidance is a gift, not a rank. Kindness and du'a for them [Field Guide ch. 17].
- *"How do I know if it's ego or sincere concern?"* Ask: would I say it privately and gently? Do I want them to do well, or do I want to be right? Would I be happy if someone else corrected them instead of me?

**Escalate:** a convert facing repeated harsh treatment or bullying at the masjid (route to the mentor or imam); anything that sounds like spiritual abuse or control.

**Don't**
- Don't name or rank specific groups as "the judgy ones."
- Don't tell the convert that someone's sin is fine; separate the act (which may be wrong) from judging the person's worth or fate.
- Don't predict anyone's afterlife (rule 9).
